data.title: Multidrug therapy (MDT) for leprosy
data.summary: Antileprosy drugs · WHO multidrug therapy regimens (blister-pack combinations of rifampicin, clofazimine, dapsone)
data.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antileprosy drugs_

**Class:** WHO multidrug therapy regimens (blister-pack combinations of rifampicin, clofazimine, dapsone)

## Mechanism of action
- Combining a bactericidal drug (rifampicin) with bacteriostatic drugs (dapsone, clofazimine) prevents resistance and kills persisters
- Monthly supervised doses ensure the key drug (rifampicin) is taken

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Classification for treatment (WHO): paucibacillary (PB) = 1–5 skin lesions, no nerve or only one nerve involved, skin smear negative; multibacillary (MB) = more than 5 lesions, or more than one nerve, or smear positive
- MB adult (12 months — 12 blister packs within 18 months): rifampicin 600 mg + clofazimine 300 mg once monthly (supervised); clofazimine 50 mg + dapsone 100 mg daily
- PB adult (older WHO/NLEP): rifampicin 600 mg monthly + dapsone 100 mg daily for 6 months (6 packs within 9 months)
- WHO 2018: the same 3 drugs for PB as well (6 months) — 'uniform' approach; India's NLEP has moved to 3-drug PB treatment (confirm current NLEP guidance)
- Children 10–14 years: rifampicin 450 mg + clofazimine 150 mg monthly; clofazimine 50 mg alternate days + dapsone 50 mg daily
- Children under 10 years: rifampicin 10 mg/kg monthly, clofazimine 100 mg monthly + 50 mg twice weekly, dapsone 2 mg/kg daily
- U-MDT (uniform MDT, trials): MB regimen for 6 months for all patients
- A-MDT (accompanied MDT): full course given at diagnosis to patients who cannot attend monthly
- ROM (rifampicin 600 mg + ofloxacin 400 mg + minocycline 100 mg) single dose — formerly for single-lesion PB; monthly ROM is an alternative regimen
- Rifampicin-resistant leprosy: clofazimine + two second-line drugs (ofloxacin/moxifloxacin, minocycline, clarithromycin) — WHO 2018
- Post-exposure prophylaxis: single-dose rifampicin (10 mg/kg, 600 mg adults) to contacts (SDR-PEP)

## Dose & formulations
- Blister packs: MB-adult (red), PB-adult (green), MB-child and PB-child packs
- Instructions to patients: take the monthly dose in front of the health worker; urine may turn red; skin will darken (clofazimine) and fade after treatment; report reactions, nerve pain, weakness early; MDT is free

## Adverse effects
- See individual drugs
- Leprosy reactions may occur during or after treatment (not a reason to stop MDT): type 1 (reversal) — prednisolone 40 mg/day tapering over 12–20 weeks; type 2 (ENL) — prednisolone, thalidomide, clofazimine

## Contraindications
- Rifampicin hypersensitivity → use alternative regimens (clofazimine + ofloxacin + minocycline)
- Dapsone allergy → MB: rifampicin + clofazimine; PB: clofazimine replaces dapsone

## Monitoring
- Monthly review: compliance, reactions, nerve function (VMT/ST), drug side effects
- Release from treatment after the fixed duration; surveillance for relapse (PB 2 years, MB 5 years per older NLEP advice)

## Pregnancy & lactation
MDT is safe and should be continued in pregnancy and breastfeeding; reactions may flare after delivery.

## Viva points
- PB vs MB definitions and regimens (adult and child doses)
- Fixed-duration therapy: MB 12 months, PB 6 months
- U-MDT, A-MDT, ROM, SDR-PEP — know what each means
- Leprosy reactions are treated without stopping MDT

## Note on sources
Leprosy regimens have changed (WHO 2018 3-drug PB; India NLEP updates). Please check the latest NLEP circular before the exam.

_Sources: Khopkar ch.6 (WHO-MDT, U-MDT, A-MDT, ROM, instructions to patients); WHO Guidelines for leprosy 2018; NLEP. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
